<reflection>
- The first experiment yielded very similar NLL values (around -24) for the vast majority of the models, with only M5 being strongly disfavored.
- This indicates that a standard reaction progress curve starting from S=2.0 and cat=0.1 without any initial product is insufficient to distinguish between standard Michaelis-Menten kinetics (M1), various deactivation pathways (M9-M20), and higher-order catalyst dependencies (M2, M13, M18, M19). My aim to establish a baseline was achieved, but it confirms that we need more extreme or specific conditions to break the degeneracy.
</reflection>
<hypothesis>
To induce divergence among the remaining plausible models, we need to probe specific mechanistic dependencies that were inactive or subtle in the first run. By introducing a high initial product concentration (P=0.5), we can strongly differentiate models with product-induced deactivation (M12, M17) from the rest, as these models will show immediate and accelerated catalyst loss. Simultaneously, increasing the catalyst concentration to its maximum (cat=0.2) will amplify the effects of second-order catalyst interactions, such as dimerization (M2) or bimolecular deactivation (M13, M18, M19), causing their kinetic profiles to scale non-linearly compared to first-order models. A moderate substrate concentration (S=1.0) ensures a balance between free catalyst and catalyst-substrate complex, allowing both free-catalyst deactivation (M9, M12, M13) and bound-catalyst deactivation (M14, M17, M18) to occur and be distinguished.
</hypothesis>
